Charles Darwin

Science · England · 1809–1882

He spent more than twenty years quietly amassing evidence before he dared publish, knowing the storm it would bring.

If you keep one line

Spend twenty years looking for what would refute you. Then publish.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Darwin changed humanity's understanding of its own place in nature more profoundly than any thinker since Copernicus. He was a comfortable, cautious gentleman-naturalist. He spent five years circling the globe aboard HMS Beagle, then two decades gathering evidence.

On the Origin of Species (1859) proposed that all living things descend, with modification, from common ancestors, and that the engine of this branching is natural selection: heritable variation winnowed by the struggle to survive and reproduce. The idea needed no designer to explain the appearance of design, and it reorganized biology into a single connected science. Everything from medicine to ecology to genetics now rests on it.

He was a meticulous, almost obsessive observer (of barnacles, earthworms, orchids, pigeons) and a gentle, anxious man tormented by the implications of his own theory. That tension between the modest naturalist and the world-shaking idea is the heart of his story.

There is unusually little to dispute here — Browne is the consensus standard. The only real caveat is length: two volumes, and no one-volume substitute is nearly as good.

02The definitive biography

Charles Darwin: Voyaging and The Power of Place (2 vols.)Janet Browne · 1995 / 2002

By near-universal agreement the biography against which all others are judged. It places the science inside the full texture of Darwin's domestic life, networks and Victorian world.
